Chapter I · Prologue

What Folklore Is, and Is Not

Folklore is not a museum of charming ideas that vanished when literacy arrived. It is the body of traditional belief, story, song, ritual, and practice that lives by transmission among ordinary people. The word itself was coined in 1846 by the English antiquarian William Thoms, who needed a single English term for what German scholars had been calling Volkskunde. The discipline that grew up around the word has been shaped, in turn, by the assumptions of each generation that took it up: nineteenth century Romantics treated folk material as the soul of a nation; twentieth century structuralists treated it as the syntax of a collective mind; today\'s historians more often treat it as evidence for how non-elite people interpreted their lives.

This study addresses Scottish folk tradition during what the historian Brian Levack calls the long early modern period, roughly 1500 to 1800, though the materials reach both earlier and later. Three traditions concern us most: the selkie of the coastal islands, the kelpie of the inland waters, and the witch belief that produced the most lethal witch-hunt per capita in early modern Europe. These three are not separate compartments. They draw on a shared substrate of liminality, on overlapping ideas about boundary-crossing beings, and on a common social world of small farming and fishing communities that needed ways to think about danger, accident, illness, and harm. Read together, they show how a single culture handled the supernatural across three quite different domains.

The Scotland that produced these traditions was not a single culture. It was, until well into the eighteenth century, two interlocking ones, separated by language, by social structure, and by a geological accident.

Chapter II · Geography

The Two Scotlands

The Highland Boundary Fault is a real geological feature, a line of crustal weakness running diagonally from Arran in the southwest to Stonehaven on the North Sea coast. It marks the southern edge of the Caledonian mountain system. North and west of the fault, the land rises into the Highlands proper: a country of mountain, sea-loch, and short steep river-courses, organized historically into kin-groups, speaking Scottish Gaelic, and practicing transhumance on poor soils. South and east lay the Lowlands: a country of rolling farmland, port cities, and burghs, organized into shires under common law, speaking Scots (the sister language to English), and orbiting around Edinburgh.

What makes this dual structure folklorically decisive is not the fault itself but the legal and ecclesiastical infrastructure that came to lie on either side of it. The kirk session, the burgh court, the sheriff court, and the Privy Council in Edinburgh: these were the institutions that made witch trials possible. They reached deep into the Lowlands and only thinly into the Highlands. The result is not that Highlanders disbelieved in witches; the local evidence shows that they did. The result is that the machinery to prosecute witches operated almost entirely in the Lowlands. Julian Goodare and the team that built the Survey of Scottish Witchcraft (2003) found that of the roughly 4,000 documented Scottish witch cases, the overwhelming majority were heard south and east of the fault.

Fig. 1The Highland Boundary Fault as cultural seam. Highland and Lowland Scotland diverged in language, land tenure, and legal reach long before the union of 1707.

The country was layered, too, by an older invasion. From the late eighth century the Norse settled the Northern Isles of Orkney and Shetland, the Western Isles of the Hebrides, and stretches of the western mainland. They held this territory for between three and seven centuries. Orkney and Shetland did not become Scottish until 1468 to 1469, when they were pledged in lieu of a dowry from Christian I of Denmark and Norway to James III of Scotland, and the pledge was never redeemed. In the Outer Hebrides, the Norse element fused with Gaelic; in the Northern Isles, it overlaid Pictish substrate and produced a distinct cultural region, with the Norse-derived language Norn still spoken in parts of Shetland into the eighteenth century.

Fig. 2The Kingdom of Mann and the Isles at its eleventh century extent. Norse political control along the Atlantic coast left a stratum of language, kinship, and folk tradition that runs through the modern record.
A Note on Linguistic Stratigraphy

Three Germanic and Celtic strata interleave in Scottish folk vocabulary. Goidelic (Gaelic) supplies words like each-uisge (water-horse), sìthichean (fairies), and cailleach (hag, old woman). Old Norse supplies selkie (seal) and most northern toponyms, including the -sker, -skaill, -vik endings of the Northern Isles. Scots, descended from Northumbrian Old English, supplies the legal and ecclesiastical vocabulary that frames the witch trials: maleficium, kirk session, warlock. The folk record can be read like a stratigraphic column: each layer is dated by its lexical content.

Chapter III · The Sea

The Selkie and the Question of Liminality

The selkie is, in the strict folkloric sense, a shapeshifter: a seal in the water and a human on land, the change effected by the removal and donning of a sealskin. The Scots and Norse-derived word simply means seal; the supernatural sense is an overlay on the ordinary one. Stories of selkie-folk are concentrated in Orkney, Shetland, the Outer Hebrides, and the Norse-influenced western mainland. They are largely absent south of the Highland line, where seal populations themselves thin out and where the coastal economy looks more to the herring than to the seal.

The standard selkie narrative belongs to what folklorists call the animal-bride tale type, classified as ATU 400 (the man on a quest for the lost wife) and ATU 402 (the supernatural bride). A fisherman or coastal farmer encounters a beautiful woman on the shore. He sees that she has removed her sealskin to walk in human shape; he steals and hides the skin; she becomes his wife and bears him children. Years later she finds the hidden skin, sometimes through the unwitting help of one of those children, and returns at once to the sea. The husband is left with the children, with a wife who looks back at them from the water, and with the recognition that she was never going to stay.

Fig. 3Selkie woman with companion seals, a contemporary illustration in the longer pictorial tradition of the seal-bride. The motif of the partially shed skin appears in iconography from the nineteenth century onward.

The structure rewards a reading through the concept of liminality, developed by the anthropologist Arnold van Gennep in Les rites de passage (1909) and elaborated by Victor Turner in the 1960s. A liminal being or place stands at a threshold: not the sea, not the land, but the shore where seal becomes woman becomes seal. Coastal communities lived their economic and biological lives at such thresholds, gathering kelp, harvesting shellfish, watching the tides, hauling boats. The selkie populates that exact zone with a story that gives it moral weight. Alan Bruford, archivist of the School of Scottish Studies, argued in Scottish Traditional Tales (1994) that selkie material survives most strongly in communities whose subsistence kept them physically on that boundary.

Fig. 4The grey seal (Halichoerus grypus) and harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) of Scottish waters. Their habit of hauling onto rocks and beaches in apparent rest, and of meeting human eye contact, contributes to the human-like reading that underlies the selkie tradition.

Several readings have circulated. The folklorist David Thomson, in The People of the Sea (1954), gathered Gaelic and Hebridean selkie testimony from informants who treated the tales with sober credence, and proposed that the stories preserved memory of contact with the Sámi or other dark-haired Scandinavian fishing peoples who occasionally appeared on Atlantic coasts. The historian John MacAulay has connected selkie genealogies in Lewis with families who claimed descent from na maighdeannan-mara, the sea-maidens, and who exhibited (so local tradition claimed) inherited skin conditions. Other readings, more psychological in inflection, take the selkie as a figure for what cannot be domesticated: the wife who never quite belongs in the marriage, the daughter who is half something else. The tales do not have to choose. They function at all of these registers at once.

Chapter IV · A Document

The Great Silkie of Sule Skerry

The most studied single selkie narrative is the ballad known to specialists as Child 113, "The Great Silkie of Sule Skerry," from Francis James Child\'s The English and Scottish Popular Ballads (five volumes, 1882 to 1898). Child took his text from a fragment collected in Orkney by Captain F. W. L. Thomas in 1852 and published in the Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland. Seven stanzas, shorter than most of its tradition: a woman nurses an unknown child, a man identifies himself as the father, he reveals that he is a selkie from Sule Skerry, he prophesies their future, and a hunter makes the prophecy true. Few ballads in the Anglo-Scottish corpus compress so much narrative into so few lines.

I am a man upon the land, I am a silkie in the sea. Child Ballad 113, Orkney variant, collected 1852

Sule Skerry itself is a real place: a forty-acre rock of Lewisian gneiss in the Atlantic, forty miles west of Orkney and thirty-five north of the Sutherland mainland. The Northern Lighthouse Board built a station there in 1895. The name is Old Norse, from súla (gannet) and sker (low rocky reef). The geography matters because, as the ballad scholar Bertrand Bronson argued in The Traditional Tunes of the Child Ballads (1959 to 1972), traditional ballads localize their supernatural figures with great specificity. The supernatural belongs to a named rock in a named sea.

Fig. 5Sule Skerry from the air. The lighthouse, automated in 1982, marks one of the most isolated rocks in the British archipelago and the named setting of the ballad collected by F. W. L. Thomas in 1852.

The ballad ends in inevitability. The selkie-father predicts that the woman will marry a hunter who will, in his trade, shoot and kill both the seal-father and the seal-child. There is no escape clause; the prophecy is not conditional. This is the formal grammar of the supernatural ballad as David Buchan described it in The Ballad and the Folk (1972): supernatural beings speak true, and what they declare is what comes. The ballad is not a horror story. It is a tragedy in the technical sense: the catastrophe is announced and then enacted, and the announcement is itself part of what makes the catastrophe complete.

Chapter V · Freshwater

The Each-Uisge and the Inland Predator

If the selkie occupies the threshold between sea and shore, the kelpie occupies the much narrower threshold between land and freshwater, and it occupies it as a predator. The Scots word kelpie is of uncertain etymology, possibly from Gaelic cailpeach or colpach, meaning a heifer or colt; the Highland Gaelic name, used across the western Highlands and the Hebrides, is each-uisge, literally "horse of the water." The same root uisge yields, through uisge beatha (water of life), the English word whisky. The water-horse and the water of life are linguistic cousins.

The kelpie appears beside a river, loch, or burn, almost always in the form of a horse, sometimes grey, sometimes black, sometimes white. It is well-groomed; sometimes a saddle and bridle are already on it. A passing traveler mounts. The hide is adhesive: once on, the rider cannot dismount. The horse rears and plunges into the water. The rider drowns. In a subset of stories the kelpie is more thoroughly predatory: the each-uisge of the great sea-lochs is said to dismember its victims, leaving only the liver to float to the surface as residue.

Fig. 6The kelpie illustrated in the late nineteenth century Romantic mode. Folk descriptions tend to be more sparing than illustrators: a fine horse, water dripping from its mane, often a saddle, always near water.

The kelpie is not, in folk-belief terms, demonic. It is amoral rather than evil. Several scholars, including Lizanne Henderson in Witchcraft and Folk Belief in the Age of Enlightenment (2016), have pressed this distinction. The kelpie operates by its own nature and not as an agent of the Devil; the witch, in the same folk world, is a human being acting under the Devil\'s instruction. The same culture held both ideas without strain. The kelpie is what the river is, fast and dangerous and impossible to bargain with. The witch is what a person can become.

The Bridle Motif

One stable element across the kelpie corpus is the bridle. A kelpie that can be approached with a bridle (often one whose buckles carry a cross stamped or scratched on them) and bridled before it can escape becomes subject to the human who holds the bridle. In some tellings the bridled kelpie can be made to plough, haul, or carry; in others, the bridle imprisons the kelpie\'s power. Remove the bridle, and the kelpie returns to the water. The motif preserves the older idea that supernatural beings can be temporarily compelled by the right ritual object but never finally domesticated. Folklorist Stewart Sanderson catalogued the bridle variants in his 1969 paper for the journal Folklore.

Chapter VI · A Primary Source

Walter Gregor and the Innerugie Bridge

The single most important nineteenth century document of kelpie belief is Walter Gregor\'s "Kelpie Stories from the North of Scotland," read to the Folk-Lore Society in London in 1883 and published the next year in the journal The Folk-Lore Record. Gregor (1825 to 1897) was a parish minister at Pitsligo on the Buchan coast and a tireless collector of northeast Scots material; his earlier Notes on the Folk-Lore of the North-East of Scotland (1881) is a foundational document of regional Scots ethnography. He recorded his sources in their own dialect.

The most famous tale in the 1883 paper concerns the building of the bridge at Innerugie in Aberdeenshire. A kelpie was caught and bridled, and the local laird (in some versions identified as Keith of Inverugie) compelled the bridled creature to haul stone from the quarry for the bridge\'s construction. When the work was complete and the bridle struck off, the kelpie, freed and furious, plunged back into the water with a curse: that the family of Keith and any rider crossing the bridge would meet ill fortune. The tale is a layered artifact. The bridge is real. The Keith family is real. The kelpie functions, in the telling, as a way of accounting for hardship and accident in a built environment, attaching specific local consequences to specific local features.

Fig. 7The horse and bridle. In folk explanation, the kelpie\'s vulnerability to a properly fitted bridle, often one inscribed or fitted with a cross, channels the older ritual idea that named or marked objects bind otherwise unbindable powers.

Gregor also recorded the well-known anecdote of the miller of Achindachy, whose mill the kelpie visited at night. The kelpie called through the door, in the local dialect, asking who was inside. The miller, who happened to be drying meal beside his pig, answered (the textual variants differ but converge): there is a pig in the mill tonight. The kelpie left. The cleverness of the tale turns on a Gaelic pun preserved through Scots translation; chattie, a pig, also serves as a teasing nickname. The kelpie is fooled not by power but by the wit of an ordinary tradesman with an ordinary domestic animal at hand. The story is not heroic. It is comic. And the comic register is significant: the kelpie is real enough to be feared but stylized enough to be defeated by a miller and a pig, which tells us something about the working theology of the rural northeast.

Chapter VII · Comparative

Cousins Across the North Sea

The Scottish water-horse is not isolated. Its closest analogues, recognized as such since the comparative folklore of John Francis Campbell in the 1860s, lie along the Atlantic and North Sea rim. The Norwegian nøkken, the German Nix or Neck, the Welsh ceffyl dŵr, and the Irish each uisce form a roughly continuous cultural belt of water-horse and water-fiddler beings whose function is much the same: to populate fresh water with personalized danger and to convert drowning into narrative.

The argument for genetic relationship, as opposed to convergent invention, rests on three lines of evidence. First, the linguistic: the Welsh, Gaelic, and Norse names share semantic structure, all building from "horse" and "water" or from a common Indo-European root for hidden, sinking, or submerging. Second, the motif: the bridle, the adhesive hide, the river-luring, the prophetic warning. Third, the geographic distribution, which tracks the medieval Norse settlement zone with high fidelity in Scotland and Iceland. Katharine Briggs, in A Dictionary of Fairies (1976), treated the water-horse as a single tradition with regional dialects rather than as four separate inventions.

Loch Ness and the Long View

The modern Loch Ness Monster tradition, which crystallized between 1933 and 1934 around sightings reported in the Inverness Courier, draws on the older substrate. The seventh century Vita Columbae, written by Adomnán of Iona between 697 and 700, includes the earliest recorded encounter with a beast in the River Ness: Saint Columba, traveling to convert the northern Picts, commands a creature to depart from a swimmer. The tale is hagiographical, not biological, but it shows the local tradition of a water-creature in this catchment to be at least 1,300 years deep. The 1933 narrative was new in form and old in template.

Chapter VIII · The Witch Belief

The Statute, the Reformation, and the Long Hunt

In 1563, three years after the Scottish Reformation Parliament had abolished papal jurisdiction in Scotland and established a Protestant kirk, the same body passed an "Anentis Witchcraftis" act. The Witchcraft Act of 1563 was short, brutal, and durable. It declared that "na maner of persoun nor persounis, of quhatsumever estate, degre, or conditioun thay be of," should practise witchcraft, sorcery, or necromancy, or consult with witches, on pain of death. It defined witchcraft as a capital crime against both God and the realm. It remained in force, with modifications, until its repeal in 1736.

Over those 173 years, by the meticulous count of the Survey of Scottish Witchcraft (Goodare, Martin, Miller, and Yeoman, 2003), Scottish authorities prosecuted roughly 4,000 individuals for witchcraft, of whom approximately 2,500 were executed. The per capita figure puts Scotland among the most lethal jurisdictions in early modern Europe, well above England and below only the small German states most notorious for the panic. The acceleration was uneven: five great panics (1590 to 1591, 1597, 1628 to 1631, 1649 to 1650, 1661 to 1662) account for the majority of executions, with calmer decades between them.

Why Scotland, and Why So Much?

Modern explanations distribute the cause across four interacting factors. First, the institutional: Scotland\'s legal procedure, unlike England\'s, permitted judicial torture on warrant from the Privy Council, and Scottish trial juries returned guilty verdicts more readily. Second, the religious: the post-Reformation Kirk, under sustained Calvinist influence, took an aggressive role in detecting witch-suspects through the kirk session, and the doctrine of the covenant placed the godly community under collective obligation to root out witch-pact. Third, the political: prosecutions intensified during periods of regime stress, including the personal rule of James VI after 1585 and the Covenanter ascendancy after 1638. Fourth, the demonological: a continental theory of the witches\' sabbath, the diabolical pact, and the witch\'s mark entered Scottish prosecution practice in the 1590s and shaped trial procedure thereafter. None of the four alone explains the Scottish pattern; their interaction does.

The historiography of Scottish witchcraft has moved through several phases. The nineteenth century, working in the wake of Robert Pitcairn\'s monumental Criminal Trials in Scotland (1829 to 1833), produced a picture of credulous ancestors and clerical fanaticism. The early twentieth century, under the influence of Margaret Murray\'s The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921), argued that what the trials recorded was an actual surviving pre-Christian fertility cult; this thesis, popular for decades, was demolished by Norman Cohn in Europe\'s Inner Demons (1975) and by subsequent archival work. The current consensus, established by Brian Levack, Goodare, and the Edinburgh school, treats witchcraft as a real social phenomenon shaped by institutional, religious, and political pressures, in which the accused were ordinary people, mostly women, mostly elderly, mostly poor.

Chapter IX · A Trial

North Berwick: The Storms and the Sabbath

In the autumn of 1589, James VI of Scotland sailed for Norway to marry, by proxy, Anne of Denmark, daughter of Frederick II. The return voyage in spring 1590 met severe storms. The fleet, including the king\'s own vessel, came near to disaster off the Norfolk coast. James and Anne reached Leith on 1 May 1590. By the end of the year a search was under way for witches who had, it was alleged, conjured the storms in an attempt to kill the new royal couple.

The case that emerged, known to history as the North Berwick witch trials of 1590 to 1591, was the first major Scottish witch panic to be conducted under the new continental theology of the diabolical pact and the witches\' sabbath. Approximately seventy people were implicated. The principal accused included Geillis Duncan (a maidservant whose torture-induced confessions named others), Agnes Sampson (an experienced midwife and healer from Haddington), John Fian (a schoolmaster at Saltpans), and the prosperous Edinburgh figure Barbara Napier. They were said, under examination, to have gathered at the parish church of North Berwick on the eve of All Hallows 1590 and to have consulted with the Devil. The Devil, they testified, had instructed them in the raising of the storms; cats had been baptized, bound to body parts of corpses, and cast into the sea; wax images of the king had been made and melted. The narrative does not require historical credence to be historically significant. It documents the form that confession was made to take.

Fig. 8James VI of Scotland and Anne of Denmark. Their 1590 storm-ridden return from Copenhagen produced the trigger event of the North Berwick prosecutions, and James\'s personal involvement reshaped Scottish witch jurisprudence for a generation.

What distinguishes North Berwick is the personal participation of the king. James attended sessions of examination at Holyrood and, by some accounts, at Edinburgh tolbooth. He questioned Agnes Sampson directly. The historian Christina Larner argued in Enemies of God (1981), the foundational modern study of the Scottish hunts, that the king\'s involvement legitimized a continental demonological framework that had previously been peripheral to Scottish practice. After North Berwick, a Scottish witch trial more often centered on the witches\' sabbath, the pact, the witch\'s mark (a supposedly insensitive spot on the body identified by pricking), and the testimony of confession extracted under sleep deprivation, "waking," and other coercive techniques formally permitted under Scottish criminal procedure. Maleficium, the doing of harm by magical means, remained important; but it now sat within a diabolical frame.

Chapter X · A Treatise

Daemonologie and the King\'s Argument

Six years after North Berwick, in 1597, the royal press in Edinburgh issued a small octavo volume titled Daemonologie, in Forme of a Dialogue. Its author, James VI, wrote it himself, in three books, between two speakers, Philomathes (the questioner) and Epistemon (the instructor). The work runs to fewer than ninety pages but states, in compact form, the king\'s settled doctrine on the reality of witchcraft, the obligation of the godly magistrate to prosecute it, and the inadequacy of skeptical positions (notably the Englishman Reginald Scot\'s The Discoverie of Witchcraft of 1584).

James argues four interlocking claims. First, witchcraft is real, not delusion; Scot is wrong. Second, witches operate by pact with the Devil; the apparent powers of magic are licit only in the sense that God permits the Devil to act through human agents. Third, the Bible commands their execution (Exodus 22:18, "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live"). Fourth, the magistrate who fails to prosecute witches breaks the covenant between godly ruler and godly people. The book is structured as a dialogue, but its rhetorical pressure runs in one direction: skepticism is moral failure. When James succeeded to the English throne in 1603 he had Daemonologie reprinted in London, and Shakespeare drew on it directly for Macbeth, written for performance at James\'s court around 1606.

The status of Daemonologie in modern scholarship has shifted. Christina Larner read it as an exemplary statement of Scottish witch-theology, and the link between royal doctrine and prosecution intensity is clear enough at the macro level. Recent work, including Stuart Clark\'s Thinking with Demons (1997) and Goodare\'s essays in The Scottish Witch-Hunt in Context (2002), reads James more cautiously: as a sophisticated theological writer working within a European framework already supplied by Jean Bodin and the Malleus Maleficarum, rather than as a uniquely Scottish innovator. James shaped the prosecution culture; he did not invent its concepts.

Chapter XI · Regional

Two Witchcrafts in One Kingdom

The geographic pattern of prosecution noted in the Survey permits a structural comparison that has become central to Scottish witchcraft historiography. The argument, in summary form, is that Highland and Lowland Scotland sustained two related but distinct witch-belief complexes, and that the two regions handled (or failed to handle) those beliefs through different institutional channels.

DimensionHighlandsLowlands
Primary languageScottish GaelicScots
Social organizationClan, kindred, transhumanceBurgh, parish, sheriff court
Religious institutionPatchy kirk presence, persistent Catholic remnantsStrong post-1560 Reformed kirk
Dominant supernatural idiomFairy belief, second sight, healing charmWitch-pact, sabbath, maleficium
Cunning folk and healersIntegrated into communal lifeIncreasingly suspect after 1590
Witch trial frequencyVery low, often locally informalHigh, court-driven, periodic panics
Use of judicial tortureRareRoutine in the panics
Primary surviving sourcesOral Gaelic tradition collected 1700s to 1900sCourt records, kirk session minutes, broadsides

The comparison is heuristic rather than absolute; Aberdeenshire (a northeast Lowland zone with significant Gaelic interface) and Argyll (a Highland zone with persistent kirk session activity) complicate it considerably. But the pattern holds well enough to support a strong claim from Henderson and Edward Cowan in Scottish Fairy Belief: A History (2001): the Highland tradition handled the supernatural through a fairy-shaped grammar in which the cunning woman and the seer were respected practitioners, while the Lowland tradition handled it through a witch-shaped grammar in which the cunning woman and the seer became, after 1590, the suspect and the accused.

Chapter XII · The Otherworld

Sìthichean: The Good Neighbors

Scottish fairy belief, called in Gaelic tradition sìthichean (singular sìthiche, from the root sìth, meaning peace, calm, or otherworld), has almost nothing in common with the diminutive winged figures of nineteenth century English picture-book fairies. The Highland sìthichean are roughly human-sized, beautiful and dangerous, living in green hills (sìtheanan, fairy mounds) and intervening in the human world with a mixture of malice, generosity, and capricious adherence to their own laws. They steal infants and leave changelings; they bless or curse cattle; they teach mortals music; they take healthy young men to dance underground for what feels like a night and proves, on return, to be a hundred years.

Highlanders avoided saying their name directly. The terms in actual use were circumlocutions: na daoine sìth (the people of peace), na daoine còire (the gentle folk), am muinntir (the people, by implication "those people"). In Scots and English, "the good neighbors," "the gentry," "the seely wights." The avoidance is itself part of the belief: to name them is to call them.

Fig. 9The fairy mound. Real Highland topography includes hundreds of small green hills, often Neolithic burial cairns long forgotten, attached in local belief to the sìthichean. The mound is the entrance to a parallel domain, and a serious risk to anyone careless enough to fall asleep on one.

The thesis that has most reshaped Scottish fairy scholarship over the last two decades comes from Lizanne Henderson and Edward J. Cowan in Scottish Fairy Belief: A History (2001) and from Emma Wilby in Cunning Folk and Familiar Spirits (2005). Their argument, working from trial records and supporting ethnographic material, holds that fairy belief and witch belief were not separate phenomena but overlapping registers of a single supernatural cosmology. The cunning woman who claimed she had received healing knowledge from the fairies, and who in her own community was a respected practitioner, became, when caught in the prosecutorial machine of the 1590s and later, a self-confessing witch with a Devil-pact. The testimony of accused women like Bessie Dunlop of Lyne (tried 1576) and Andro Man of Aberdeen (tried 1597) makes this overlap explicit: both described relations with a fairy or "Queen of Elfame" figure, and both were prosecuted as witches under the 1563 statute.

The Witch and the Fairy: One Argument

Henderson and Cowan press a strong claim. The continental demonological framework, imported through North Berwick and intensified by James VI\'s Daemonologie, did not replace an empty cosmology. It overwrote a working fairy cosmology in which contact with the otherworld was the routine basis of cunning craft. The judges, trained in continental theology, heard "Queen of Elfame" and wrote "the Devil." The accused, often illiterate and now under torture, learned the new vocabulary fast. The result is that the trial records preserve, in distorted form, the language of a fairy belief system that the elite prosecutors were systematically failing to recognize as such. Reading the records against the grain, as Wilby does, recovers that older substrate.

Chapter XIII · The Older Layer

The Cailleach and the Pre-Christian Substrate

Beneath the fairy belief sits a still older stratum. The Gaelic cailleach (literally "old woman," "veiled one," from caille, veil) names a figure who is not exactly a goddess and not exactly a folk personification, but who carries traces of both. The Cailleach Bheur, the Blue Hag of winter, is associated with snow, mountains, storms, and the wild high ground; she is said in numerous Highland topographies to have shaped landscapes by dropping stones from her apron or by quarrying mountains with a hammer. Her opposite number is Brìghde, the bright one, whose feast on 1 February (Imbolc, Là Fhèill Brìghde) marks the turning of winter to spring.

The cailleach figure is unevenly Christianized. In some Argyll and Hebridean traditions she is treated as a saint, blessed and benevolent; in others she retains a frankly pagan ferocity. Anne Ross in Pagan Celtic Britain (1967) and Ronald Black in The Gaelic Otherworld (2005) both treat the cailleach as evidence for the survival, within Gaelic Christian practice, of a pre-Christian female personification of the wild and ungoverned. The category is not "pagan survival" in the simple sense; it is what the religious historian Ronald Hutton calls syncretism, the practical layering of religious systems in everyday devotional life.

The clootie well (Gaelic tobar nan ròpan, "well of the strips"), at sites like the Clootie Well at Munlochy on the Black Isle, offers a particularly clear case. Pilgrims dipped a strip of cloth in the well, tied it to a tree, and walked away; as the cloth weathered, the illness was said to depart with it. The practice is documented from medieval Christian use, but its structure (a sacred water, a tree, a deposit, an exchange) predates the Christian frame by centuries. Alexander Carmichael, collecting in the late nineteenth century, recorded blessings for use at such wells in which a saint\'s name was invoked over a ritual whose form was older than the saint.

Fig. 10A traditional blackhouse village in the Outer Hebrides. Until well into the twentieth century, communities like Arnol on Lewis sustained the ceilidh, a household gathering at which traditional tales, music, and lore circulated across generations.
Chapter XIV · The Sources

Voices in the Record

Almost everything we can say about Scottish folk tradition before the twentieth century reaches us through a small number of named collectors. They are not transparent windows. Each brought his (almost always his) own framework, theological commitments, antiquarian interests, and editorial conventions to the material. The historiography of Scottish folklore is, in significant part, the historiography of these intermediaries.

c. 1691 (Published 1815)
Robert Kirk, minister of Aberfoyle, completes the manuscript The Secret Commonwealth of Elves, Fauns, and Fairies, a sympathetic ethnography of Highland fairy belief by an educated Gaelic-speaking cleric. It circulates in manuscript and is finally printed by Walter Scott in 1815.
1801 to 1803
Walter Scott, Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border. Influential as model and as canon-builder, but freely emended and reshaped its source ballads. Modern scholarship treats it with skepticism on textual fidelity.
1829 to 1833
Robert Pitcairn, Criminal Trials in Scotland, 1488 to 1624, three volumes. Transcribes surviving witch trial records; the foundational primary source corpus for the prosecution history.
1860 to 1862
John Francis Campbell of Islay, Popular Tales of the West Highlands, four volumes. Recorded in Gaelic with parallel English. Methodologically rigorous for its time, with named informants and source-fidelity.
1881, 1883
Walter Gregor, Notes on the Folk-Lore of the North-East of Scotland and "Kelpie Stories from the North of Scotland." Northeast Scots material in dialect, parish-minister fieldwork.
1882 to 1898
Francis James Child, The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, five volumes. The standard reference corpus of 305 numbered ballads, including Child 113, the Sule Skerry ballad.
1900 to 1971
Alexander Carmichael, Carmina Gadelica, six volumes. Hebridean Gaelic charms, prayers, and folk material; first two volumes 1900, remaining four published posthumously by descendants. Recent scholarship (notably John MacInnes) has shown that Carmichael substantially edited and recombined his sources, raising textual-critical questions about the published corpus.
1951
The School of Scottish Studies is founded at the University of Edinburgh. Systematic audio fieldwork begins, including Hamish Henderson\'s recordings of Scottish travellers and Calum Maclean\'s Hebridean work. The first generation of recorded oral tradition.
2003
The Survey of Scottish Witchcraft goes online (Goodare, Martin, Miller, Yeoman). For the first time, the full prosecution record is electronically searchable and statistically analyzable.

The collectors are not equivalent to the tradition. They are filtered, partial, sometimes substantially reshaped. Modern Scottish folklore scholarship spends much of its time reading these archives critically: against each other, against the trial records, against later oral recordings, against material culture. The recovered picture is messier than any single collector\'s, and more interesting.

Chapter XV · The Performance

The Ceilidh and the Living Text

To understand any of this material is to understand that it was, for most of its history, performed rather than read. The Gaelic ceilidh (from ceilidh, "a visit") was, until the dispersal of Highland communities in the nineteenth century clearances and twentieth century emigration, the routine evening institution of rural Scotland. Neighbors gathered at a designated house, often the household of a recognized tradition-bearer, and the evening filled with story, song, riddle, news, and music. The Hebridean ceilidh was not staged. It was the medium in which folk tradition reproduced itself.

Calum Maclean, in fieldwork carried out for the Irish Folklore Commission in South Uist and Eriskay between 1946 and 1949, identified specific tradition-bearers whose repertoire of long Gaelic prose tales ran to hundreds of items, performed without script and with consistent narrative architecture across multiple recordings. The work of Albert Lord and Milman Parry on Yugoslav oral epic in the 1930s had argued that such performance operates not through verbatim memorization but through what they called oral-formulaic composition: the bearer composes the tale anew at each performance, deploying stock phrases, themes, and structural patterns. Maclean\'s Hebridean material substantially confirms the Parry-Lord model for the Gaelic context.

The implication for textual study is considerable. There is no single "correct" version of a folk tale. There are versions, related by genealogy and performance, drifting in and out of contact with one another. The variants of "The Great Silkie of Sule Skerry" recorded in Orkney in 1852, in Shetland in the early twentieth century, and in modern revivalist performance are not corruptions of an original. They are siblings in a performance lineage. The selkie-mother who weeps when she finds her skin in one telling is grimly silent in another, not because either teller misremembered, but because each performance produces the tale to a specific audience on a specific evening.

This frame matters for how the witch material should be read too. The confession of Agnes Sampson at Holyrood in 1591 is not a verbatim transcript of a sustained life-story. It is a co-produced text, generated in the encounter between an examined witness, a panel of examiners with their own theological agenda, a scribe with limited dialect competence, and the physical pressures of sleep deprivation and pricking. Emma Wilby\'s The Visions of Isobel Gowdie (2010) is the most sustained recent attempt to read such a record as the layered composition it is.

Chapter XVI · The Reinvention

Steel Horses: The Falkirk Kelpies

In April 2014, sculptor Andy Scott\'s monumental work The Kelpies, unveiled in 2013 at the Helix park near Falkirk, opened to the public. Two horse-head sculptures rise thirty meters from the basin of the Forth and Clyde Canal: the height of a ten-story building, in welded steel, each composed of 928 plates over an internal frame. They are now among the most photographed objects in Scotland and the most visited public artworks in the United Kingdom.

Fig. 11Andy Scott\'s The Kelpies at the Helix park, Falkirk, unveiled 2013. Modeled on two real Clydesdale horses (Duke and Baron), the sculpture interlaces the older water-horse tradition with the labor history of Scotland\'s canal era.

Scott\'s reading of the kelpie tradition for this commission deserves attention as an act of public folklore-translation. The sculpture references the each-uisge of myth, but it does so through the explicit additional figure of the Clydesdale, the working draft horse of nineteenth and early twentieth century Scotland. Two named Clydesdales, Duke and Baron, were the live models. The pairing collapses two registers, the mythic water-horse and the actual heavy horse that hauled barges, ploughed fields, and powered canal traffic, into one civic symbol. The placement, at a critical canal junction in central Scotland\'s industrial heartland, is part of the argument.

The cultural-studies reading of public folklore commissions like The Kelpies, developed by Cristina Bacchilega in Folktales Transformed (2013) and by Diane Purkiss in earlier work on witch-figure reception, treats them as instances of folklorization: the deliberate, often state-supported repurposing of folk tradition for contemporary cultural and economic purposes (tourism, national identity, place-marketing, civic pride). The kelpie at Falkirk is not the kelpie of Aberdeenshire farmers in 1883. It is, by intention, a new object that draws its authority from the old one. Folklorization is neither a betrayal of tradition nor a continuation of it; it is a different operation that uses traditional material as raw stock.

Chapter XVII · Synthesis

What the Stories Were For

It is tempting, at the end of an introductory survey, to ask what Scottish folk tradition was "really" about. The question is not quite the right one. Tradition is not a code that contains a single message awaiting decryption. It is, in Carlo Ginzburg\'s formulation in The Cheese and the Worms (1976), a layered cultural practice that does multiple kinds of work for the communities that sustain it. The selkie, the kelpie, the fairy, and the witch each did several things at once.

They named risk and gave it a face. The seal-strewn coasts of Orkney lost fishermen; the freshwater lochs of the Highlands took drinkers and travelers; the elderly women of small parishes lived under suspicion when crops failed or children sickened. To attach a story to the danger is to make it negotiable, to convert the meaningless into the addressable. Folklore does not eliminate accident, but it gives accident a grammar.

They preserved boundary work. The selkie, the changeling, the cunning woman, the witch: each defines, by transgression, where the boundary of the human community lies. The boundary is not absolute. It can be crossed in either direction; people sometimes return from the otherworld, and sometimes do not. The persistence of these figures across centuries is partly a function of how useful boundary-marking remains, even when the precise edges shift.

They sustained a record of cultural contact. The Norse layer in selkie geography, the continental theology that shaped the trials, the Gaelic substrate visible in the cailleach and the sìthichean: each of these is sedimentary evidence of historical contact between cultural systems. Folklore preserves what archives do not. The selkie ballad records the maritime contact zone between Orkney and Scandinavia better than any state document.

They handled, in modes the conscious record could not, what mattered most about being human in a hard place. The fragility of fishing economies, the inevitability of accident, the contingency of childbirth and recovery, the limits of human knowledge: these were lived realities for the communities the collectors reached. The stories were a discipline of attention to them.

The Scottish material is unusual in that we can read all of this at once. The witch trial records survive in legible quantity; the oral tradition was collected, however imperfectly, by named individuals working between 1690 and 1971; the geographic and linguistic patterns can be mapped; the modern reinventions are visible in the public landscape. Few national traditions yield this complete a documentary trail. To read it carefully is to recover the working cultural history of a country that was, for a long time, two countries; that built one of the most lethal witch-prosecution systems in Europe; and that simultaneously preserved, in Gaelic and in Scots, one of the most richly textured supernatural cosmologies in the European archive.

An t-eòlach air a' bhliadhna a dh'fhalbh
